title: Fighting to Expand the Margins of Journalism in Egypt

_By Lina Attalah_

CAIRO, Egypt--On October 27, I stood before a judge in a courtroom in Cairo
with my defense team of eight committed lawyers beside me. A week earlier, I
had been summoned for interrogation on charges of running a website without a
license. It was the sixth time over the last few years that I had faced
prosecutorial questioning. But it was the first time I was referred to court.

At the beginning of the court session, the judge repeatedly assured us that
this was a small, simple case; it shouldn't be a big deal. Apparently for this
judge, and for others with power, shutting down Egypt's leading independent
newsroom was not a big deal. As the trial proceeded, all of our defense team's
requests were summarily rejected, including requests for time to prepare a
defense, submit additional documents, or to summon witnesses. As the space in
the courtroom was being increasingly void of law, the judge decided to ignore
all my lawyers and instead appointed a lawyer to take up my defense. I
objected, my eight lawyers objected, and the judge proceeded to pronounce his
ruling in this small, simple case, as I was being forcibly carried by
policemen out of the courtroom. I didn't get to hear the verdict.

After seven hours in dark, musty custody, I learned from a paper that I had to
sign to be released that the court ordered Mada Masr to be shut down and
imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds. Just like that, 13 years of
journalism practice had ended in a five-minute judicial performance.

That day in court came at the tail end of various other encounters with the
law, where we took every initiative possible to avoid that outcome. A media
law was passed in 2018 ordering us to get licensed. We applied right away but
did not get a response. In 2020, when the legislation's bylaws were finally
published, we applied again. Again, we did not get a response, despite the law
obligating the licensing authority to provide a response within a 90-day
period of the application. In 2022, we learned during an interrogation session
at the public prosecutor's office that in fact, our license had been rejected,
a decision that was never addressed to us and never included any reasoning.
Nonetheless, we contested the decision at the State Council and when that
contestation was rejected, we resubmitted our application with additional
paperwork. We have received no response from authorities since 2023.
Recounting these details is only an index for how we have always tried to stay
within the bounds of a law designed to control, rather than to regulate.

Our battle has not just been to do independent journalism, but to institute in
a sustainable way--including through legal practice--the expansion of the
space allowed for us and others to operate.

* * *

In 2013, we, a group of journalists from Cairo, came together to create Mada
Masr in a moment of political turmoil. Regime change was at the door, followed
a year later by the election of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi. Thirteen years
ensued of heavily tightened political rule with very little spaces of politics
left, including power politics, and a rising integration in the global economy
as one of many debt-drunk "emerging" markets, all in the midst of a radically
shifting region.

That summer of 2013, the urge was to understand the moment, to give it shape
in thinking and writing, to create a record of it. In doing so, we sought to
keep people engaged in these transformations, and to find the connections
between them and their daily lives. This is the space of politics we have been
building over the last 13 years.

In our minds, journalism has always been a vocational space through which we
can resist the active cancellation of politics. In times where this
cancellation is manifested in the removal of spaces and people--
unrepresentative parliaments, powerless opposition parties, fractured civil
society, jailed regime opponents, propagandist media--independent journalism,
with Mada Masr at the forefront of it in Egypt, kept some of this space alive.
The substance of this space is asking questions, finding answers, thinking
about them, and presenting all of it to the public, which enlarges the scope
of the questions and the answers. It's the dynamism of thinking that keeps
life political.

Keeping our life political, living our life politically, is a way to assert
the legitimacy of our existence as a people; a legitimacy that transforms our
need for dignified life into a right.

Over these past 13 years, we have been working, and over our heads, a chorus
was repeating at Egyptians, at times shouting at us: that those in power know
it all, that the stability of our country lies in their hands alone, that we
should just mind our own business (business here is strictly tied to putting
food on the table if you are from the middle class and below), that we are too
needy, that many sacrifices are made for us. At Mada Masr, we simply chose to
ignore the shouting, and do the work.

Today, it is not surprising to find ourselves being punished because we
ignored the shouting. This is why we now find ourselves under a storm of
targeted shouting.

And this is why we are fighting to expand that margin of space for us and
others to operate. And this is why we still hold on to our right for appeal,
with a court date set for November 25.

And this is how we will go back to court next week, on November 11. Because
upon my release last week, I learned that I had been convicted in absentia in
2024 on charges of publishing "false" news and running a website without a
license (again) and sentenced to one year imprisonment and (another) LE2
million fine. The ruling was handed down in absentia even though I always
lived in the country. They had charged me and tried me and never told me. We
will go back to court this week, and we will try to push for our defense
statements to be made; this time adding that journalists should not be jailed,
not only as a moral position, but also as a right inscribed in Egypt's
constitution.

And because journalists should not be jailed, and because there is no
individual salvation in a context like this, we hope to come out of this court
session free, but also followed and preceded by another 26 journalists behind
bars. The latest of these imprisonments are six young journalists, some of
whom I have personally mentored, and together, they made up the entire
newsroom of the fact-checking platform Matsadaash.

I hope to come out of court next week, and make it back to our newsroom, and
stay there until the late hours of the day trying to understand, report,
write, further institute, and have coffee with young journalists, including
with those of Matsadaash, who made their entry into our world with the magical
double "C": curiosity and courage. These are the substances of political
living that we are fighting not to lose.

_Lina Attalah is the co-founder and editor-in-chief of Mada Masr. She lives in
Cairo, Egypt. For press inquiries, contact mada@madamasr.com._
